topic: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
parentTitle: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
title: Recognising deterioration in people with a learning disability
blurb: Spot deterioration early by knowing the person's baseline, acting on soft signs and carer concern, and interpreting NEWS2 without diagnostic overshadowing.
question: Peter, 45, has a severe learning disability and is on a medical ward with a urinary infection. His sister says, 'He's not himself, he's gone quiet and won't hold his cup.' His NEWS2 score is 2. A colleague says his observations are fine. What should the nurse do?

teach.body: People with a learning disability may not be able to say they feel worse, may show illness through behaviour, and may have physical features that make observations harder to read. LeDeR and CIPOLD found delays in recognising illness, in tests and in treatment, and that families' concerns were not acted on. In plain English: the early warning often comes from the people who know the person, before the numbers change.

head: Area
Possible soft sign
rows: Eating or drinking less, refusing favourites
Not walking, dropping things, needing more help
teach.caption: A soft sign only means something against what is usual for this person.

teach.body: NEWS2 applies to adults with a learning disability, but it supports and never replaces clinical judgement, and should be interpreted in the context of the person's usual physiology and conditions. Find out the person's baselines on admission from the hospital passport and family: usual observations, behaviour, communication, eating, mobility and how they show pain. NICE NG253 also says consider higher risk if the person has deteriorated or not improved since a previous score.

teach.caption: Carer concern or a soft sign is a reason to escalate even when the score is low.
Martha's Rule: patients, families and carers can request a review from a different team if worried and not responded to.

teach.body: Peter's sister knows his baseline: he normally chats, feeds himself and holds his cup. Going quiet and dropping his cup are soft signs. The nurse thanks her, repeats a full ABCDE assessment and finds his respiratory rate is now 22 and he is passing little urine. She escalates to the doctor with SBAR, describing the change from his baseline, not just the NEWS2. A sepsis review follows. She records the soft signs and tells his sister how to raise concerns again, including through Martha's Rule.

teach.text: Diagnostic overshadowing: putting new behaviour, drowsiness or distress down to the learning disability ('that's just how he is'). New agitation, withdrawal or self-injury can be pain, infection, constipation or hypoxia. NICE NG253 says changes in cognitive function may present as changes in behaviour or irritability in adults with a learning disability (1.4.8), and lists a history from a friend or relative of new altered behaviour among its medium-risk criteria for sepsis outside hospital.

letters.word: Recommendation: review within a set time

items: Ask the person and family how observations can be done with least distress.
Use the hospital passport and the Reasonable Adjustment Digital Flag.
Let family stay to help with observations and reassurance.
Use DisDAT or the person's known pain cues when they cannot report pain.
Involve the learning disability liaison nurse early.
Know the baseline: observations, behaviour, eating, mobility, pain cues.
Soft signs and carer concern are triggers to reassess and escalate.
NEWS2 supports, never replaces, judgement; worsening since the last score means higher risk.
Avoid diagnostic overshadowing: behaviour change may be illness or pain.
Escalate with SBAR; families can use Martha's Rule.

summary: You can now find and use a person's baseline, recognise soft signs of deterioration and act on carer concern. You can interpret NEWS2 alongside clinical judgement, avoid diagnostic overshadowing and escalate clearly.

A.q: In a supported living service, staff ask what 'soft signs' of deterioration might look like for Lena, 33, who has a profound learning disability. Which example fits best?
options: A respiratory rate of 26 breaths per minute
Eating less and sleeping more than usual
A NEWS2 score of 7 on a set of observations
Oxygen saturation of 89% on room air
A.why: Soft signs are subtle changes from the person's baseline, such as eating, sleeping, mobility and behaviour, that may come before vital signs change.

whyNot.0: A raised respiratory rate is a measured vital sign, not a soft sign.
whyNot.2: A NEWS2 of 7 is a high score needing emergency response, not a soft sign.
whyNot.3: Low saturation is a measured physiological sign.

A.q: A ward is admitting Mohammed, 44, who has a learning disability. The nurse wants to recognise deterioration early. Which information is most useful to gather on admission?
options: His usual baselines from family and his passport
A list of his previous hospital admissions
His level of learning disability in his notes
His preferred television programmes, music and food
A.why: Knowing usual observations, behaviour, eating, sleeping, mobility and pain cues lets staff recognise change. Family and passports are key sources.

whyNot.1: Past admissions help but do not describe what is normal for him.
whyNot.2: Severity does not tell you his individual baseline.
whyNot.3: Preferences help comfort but do not show deterioration.

A.q: Who is often the first to notice early deterioration in a person with a learning disability who has limited speech?
options: The consultant on the weekly ward round
The pharmacist reviewing the drug chart
The bed manager planning discharges
Family carers and regular support staff
A.why: People who know the person's baseline notice subtle changes first; LeDeR and CIPOLD show their concerns must be acted on.

whyNot.0: A weekly round is too infrequent to see subtle day-to-day change.
whyNot.1: Pharmacists review medicines, not daily behaviour.
whyNot.2: Bed managers do not observe the person's baseline.

B.q: Peter, 45, has a severe learning disability and a urinary infection. His sister says, 'He's not himself, he's gone quiet.' His NEWS2 is 2. What should the nurse do?
options: Reassure her that his score is in the low range
Act on her concern, reassess fully and escalate
Record her comment and recheck at the next round
Ask her to tell the doctor on the morning round
B.why: Family know his baseline and often notice soft signs before scores change. NEWS2 supports, never replaces, clinical judgement; concern triggers reassessment and escalation.

whyNot.0: False reassurance ignores a key early warning.
whyNot.3: The nurse is responsible for escalating, not the family.

B.q: Amira, 50, has a profound learning disability. Her NEWS2 has risen from 2 to 5 over four hours, and her carers say she is 'not right'. What response does NEWS2 require?
options: Continue the same observations every 4 to 6 hours
Repeat the full set of observations in 12 hours
Emergency call to the critical care outreach team
Urgent clinical review and hourly observations
B.why: A NEWS2 of 5 or more is the key threshold for an urgent response: at least hourly observations and urgent review by a clinician with core competencies in acute illness.

whyNot.0: 4-6 hourly is for scores of 1 to 4.
whyNot.2: An emergency critical care response is for 7 or more.

B.q: Lucas, 41, has a severe learning disability and is admitted with vomiting. Staff note he is shouting more and pushing staff away when they touch his abdomen, which is distended. A colleague says, 'That's his challenging behaviour.' What should the nurse do?
options: Give his prescribed PRN medicine for agitation
Ask security to support his care
Leave him to settle in a side room
Complete an ABCDE assessment and escalate
B.why: Vomiting, a distended abdomen and new distress on touch suggest a serious problem such as obstruction. The behaviour is likely communicating pain; assessment and escalation are needed.

whyNot.0: Sedating him could mask a surgical emergency.
whyNot.1: Security does not address the likely physical cause.
whyNot.2: Leaving him risks missing an abdominal emergency.

C.q: Jack, 34, has a learning disability and lives in a care home. Over three days staff notice he is eating less, sleeping more and needs help walking, which is new. His observations are within normal ranges. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Record soft signs and seek a GP review today
Continue to monitor and recheck in one week
Encourage more activity to improve his walking
Contact his family to ask if this is new
C.why: A cluster of soft signs over several days is an early warning even when vital signs are normal. Recording them against his baseline and seeking same-day review prevents delay.

whyNot.2: Encouraging activity ignores a possible illness.
whyNot.3: Staff already know it is new; the priority is medical review.

C.q: Rosa, 29, has a learning disability. Her NEWS2 was 3 at 10:00 and is 4 at 14:00, with her respiratory rate rising each time. She has been on antibiotics for 24 hours. According to NICE NG253, how should this be interpreted?
options: As low risk, because the score is under 5
As a likely side effect of her antibiotics
As higher risk than the score alone suggests
As expected after only 24 hours of treatment
C.why: NG253 1.6.4: consider a higher risk than NEWS2 suggests if there has been deterioration or no improvement since a previous score or intervention.

whyNot.0: The worsening trend matters as well as the number.
whyNot.1: Nothing points to an antibiotic reaction.
whyNot.3: A rising score after treatment is not expected and needs review.

C.q: Danny, 36, has a learning disability and pneumonia. His mother has raised concerns twice that he is getting worse, but she feels the team have not responded. What should the nurse tell her?
options: She should wait until the consultant's ward round
She can make a formal complaint after discharge
She can request a review from a different team
She should ask his GP to contact the ward
C.why: Martha's Rule gives patients, families and carers an escalation route to request a review from a different team when worried and not responded to. The nurse should also escalate the concern herself.

whyNot.0: Waiting delays action on a concern about deterioration.
whyNot.1: A complaint after discharge does not help Danny now.
whyNot.3: The GP is not part of the inpatient escalation route.

reteach.title: The person's normal is the reference range
reteach.question: Why might a 'normal' set of observations still hide a person who is becoming seriously ill?

blocks.body: Numbers (NEWS2) and knowledge of the person (baseline, soft signs, carer concern). Each can show deterioration the other misses. When a family member who knows the person says 'something's wrong', treat it like an abnormal observation: reassess and escalate.

blocks.text: 'It's just his behaviour' is a sentence that has preceded avoidable deaths. Assume a physical cause until it is ruled out.

explain.body: Collect on admission: usual observations, communication, behaviour, eating, sleeping, mobility and how the person shows pain, from the hospital passport and family.

test.q: What is the main reason for recording a person's baseline on admission?
options: To complete the admission paperwork on time
To judge which ward is most suitable
To recognise change from what is usual
To decide the severity of the disability
test.why: A baseline lets staff recognise deterioration as a change from what is usual for this person.

whyNot.1: Ward allocation is a separate decision.
whyNot.3: Severity is not assessed this way.

explain.body: Eating, drinking, sleeping, mobility, behaviour, continence or appearance changing from usual. They may come before vital signs change.

test.q: Which is a soft sign of deterioration?
options: Systolic BP of 88 mmHg
New reluctance to walk
Heart rate of 132
SpO2 of 90% on air
test.why: A new reluctance to walk is a change in usual function, a soft sign.

whyNot.0: This is a measured vital sign.
whyNot.2: This is a measured vital sign.
whyNot.3: This is a measured vital sign.

explain.body: 0: minimum 12-hourly. 1-4: low, 4-6 hourly. 3 in one parameter: urgent ward review. 5-6: urgent response. 7+: emergency response with critical care skills.

test.q: A man with a learning disability scores 3 for respiratory rate alone, with an aggregate NEWS2 of 3. What response is required?
options: Routine 12-hourly observations
Emergency critical care team
Urgent ward-based review
No change until the score is 5
test.why: A score of 3 in any single parameter triggers a low-medium, urgent ward-based response with at least hourly observations.

whyNot.1: Emergency response is for 7 or more.
whyNot.3: A single 3 already triggers an urgent response.

explain.body: Attributing new symptoms or behaviour to the learning disability so illness is missed. Treat behaviour change as possible pain or illness until proven otherwise.

options: 'Her shouting is just part of her LD'
'Let's check her bowels and obs first'
'Her mum says this is not usual for her'
'She may be showing us she is in pain'
test.why: Attributing new behaviour to the learning disability without looking for a cause is diagnostic overshadowing.

whyNot.1: This looks for a physical cause.
whyNot.2: This uses the family's knowledge of her baseline.
